claims.text: Conventional quenched and tempered martensitic Cr–Mo steel can exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition across a narrow tempering-temperature window.
Temper embrittlement in martensitic Cr–Mo steel arises from diffusion-controlled segregation of impurity elements to grain boundaries.
Phosphorus is an example of an impurity that segregates to grain boundaries in this steel.
Finely spaced tempering temperatures and durations can first induce and then reverse solute-segregation effects.
At lower tempering temperatures, diffusion is limited.
At intermediate tempering temperatures, impurity segregation occurs and causes embrittlement.
At higher tempering temperatures, recovery reduces segregation.
Phosphorus segregation at grain boundaries is the structural mediator of the transition.
Intermediate tempering temperatures provide sufficient atomic mobility for phosphorus to segregate to grain boundaries.
Weakening of intergranular cohesion by phosphorus causes a marked loss of ductility.
At lower temperatures, diffusion is too slow to produce significant phosphorus segregation.
At higher temperatures, dissolution or redistribution of phosphorus restores ductility.
Ductility should display a pronounced minimum in the intermediate tempering regime relative to lower and higher temperature regimes.
The as-quenched and over-tempered states typically have high ductility because segregation effects are minimal or reversed.
The transition occurs only within a narrow temperature-time window determined by alloy chemistry.
Changes in impurity concentration or tempering parameters may shift or suppress the transition.
